Back: Telnet (port 23) → SSH (port 22). Telnet sends keystrokes including passwords in plaintext. SSH encrypts all traffic. Exam trap: if scenario needs 'secure remote CLI access', answer is SSH, not Telnet.
HTTP (port 80) → HTTPS (port 443). HTTP sends data in cleartext. HTTPS adds TLS encryption + certificate validation. Exam trap: a login page served over HTTP is ALWAYS a vulnerability.

FTP (ports 20/21) → SFTP (port 22) or FTPS (ports 989/990). FTP sends credentials + data in plaintext. SFTP uses SSH. FTPS uses TLS. Exam trap: SFTP ≠ FTPS — different protocols despite similar names.
POP3 (port 110) → POP3S (port 995). POP3 downloads email unencrypted. POP3S wraps in TLS. Exam trap: POP3 deletes from server after download — no multi-device sync.
IMAP (port 143) → IMAPS (port 993). IMAP keeps mail on server, syncs across devices. IMAPS encrypts. Exam trap: scenario says 'access email from phone and laptop' → IMAPS, not POP3S.

SMTP (port 25) → SMTPS (port 465) or SMTP+STARTTLS (port 587). Port 25 is unauthenticated relay. Port 587 requires auth + supports TLS upgrade. Exam trap: 25 = server-to-server, 587 = client-to-server submission.
LDAP (port 389) → LDAPS (port 636). LDAP binds send BIND request with password. LDAPS encrypts entire LDAP session. Exam trap: LDAPS uses dedicated port 636, not STARTTLS on 389.
SNMPv1/v2c (port 161) → SNMPv3 (port 161). v1/v2c use community strings (plaintext 'public'). v3 adds encryption + authentication. Exam trap: SNMPv3 uses same port 161 — different version, same port.
PPTP (port 1723) → L2TP/IPsec (ports 1701/UDP + 500/UDP + 4500/UDP) or IKEv2 (500/4500) or SSTP (443). PPTP uses MPPE encryption (broken). L2TP/IPsec provides actual security.
VNC (port 5900) → RDP with NLA (port 3389) or SSH tunneling. VNC has no native encryption. RDP with Network Level Authentication (NLA) requires pre-authentication before session.

Front: Which protocol provides file integrity verification?
Back: Hashing algorithms: SHA-256 (secure), SHA-3 (latest), SHA-2 family. NOT MD5 (collision attacks), SHA-1 (deprecated). Exam trap: hashing verifies integrity, encryption provides confidentiality.

Encryption: AES-256 (symmetric, bulk data), RSA/ECC (asymmetric, key exchange/digital signatures), ChaCha20 (mobile/IoT). Exam trap: symmetric = same key both ends, fast. Asymmetric = key pair, slower, used for key exchange.

Digital signatures. Sender signs hash of message with private key. Recipient verifies with public key. Provides: authentication (proves sender), integrity (hash unchanged), non-repudiation (sender cannot deny).

Front: Which protocol should replace deprecated SSL 3.0/TLS 1.0?
Back: TLS 1.2 or TLS 1.3. SSL 3.0 (POODLE attack), TLS 1.0 (BEAST), TLS 1.1 (deprecated). TLS 1.3 removes insecure cipher suites, reduces handshake round trips (1-RTT vs 2-RTT). Exam trap: always choose TLS 1.2+ for 'secure' transport.

WPA3 replaces WPA2. WPA2 uses 4-way handshake with Pre-Shared Key (vulnerable to dictionary attack via captured handshake). WPA3 uses SAE (Simultaneous Authentication of Equals) — provides forward secrecy + offline dictionary attack protection.

Front: Email authentication: SPF vs DKIM vs DMARC?
Back: SPF: TXT record listing authorized sending IPs (envelope spoofing). DKIM: digital signature on email headers (content tampering). DMARC: policy telling receivers what to do if SPF/DKIM fail (p=none, p=quarantine, p=reject). Exam trap: ALL three needed for anti-spoofing.

Diffie-Hellman: two parties establish shared secret over insecure channel. Provides forward secrecy (ephemeral keys). RSA key exchange: encrypts pre-master secret with server's public key. No forward secrecy. Exam trap: DHE/ECDHE preferred over RSA key exchange for PFS.

802.1X: port-based NAC using EAP authentication (RADIUS backend). Each device must authenticate before accessing network. MAC filtering: allowlist MAC addresses — trivially spoofed. Exam trap: 802.1X is real security. MAC filtering is NOT security.

Front: Cloud security: CASB vs CSPM vs CWPP?
Back: CASB (Cloud Access Security Broker): visibility + control between users and cloud apps (shadow IT). CSPM (Cloud Security Posture Mgmt): detects cloud misconfigurations (S3 bucket open). CWPP (Cloud Workload Protection Platform): protects VMs/containers workloads.

Front: Authentication: SAML vs OIDC vs OAuth 2.0?
Back: SAML: XML-based SSO for enterprise apps (ADFS, Okta). OIDC (OpenID Connect): JSON-based SSO over OAuth 2.0 for modern apps. OAuth 2.0: authorization delegation ONLY (not auth). Exam trap: SAML = enterprise SSO, OIDC = modern/mobile SSO, OAuth = API permissions.

RADIUS: IETF standard AAA. UDP ports 1812/1813. Encrypts only password. Combines auth + authorization. Used for 802.1X, VPN, WPA-Enterprise. TACACS+: Cisco proprietary. TCP port 49. Encrypts entire packet. Separates auth, authorization, accounting.

IDS (Intrusion Detection System): passive monitoring, alerts on anomalies. No traffic blocking. IPS (Intrusion Prevention System): inline, can block malicious traffic in real-time. Exam trap: IDS = monitor + alert. IPS = monitor + block. Never pick IDS when scenario requires blocking.

Stateless: filters each packet independently — no connection tracking. Fast but can't detect out-of-state packets. Stateful: tracks connection state (SYN→SYN-ACK→ACK). Allows return traffic automatically. Knows if packet belongs to established connection. Exam trap: stateful is default modern firewall.

WAF (Web Application Firewall): Layer 7, protects web apps from SQLi, XSS, CSRF. Understands HTTP/HTTPS. NGFW (Next-Gen Firewall): combines stateful firewall + IPS + app awareness. WAF sits in front of web servers. NGFW at network perimeter.

Front: VPN: Site-to-site vs Remote access vs Clientless?
Back: Site-to-site: connects two networks (IPsec tunnel between gateways). Remote access: user device to network (VPN client). Clientless: browser-based SSL VPN (no software — uses HTML5/Java). Exam trap: ZTNA is replacing traditional VPN for remote access (app-level vs network-level).

TLS 1.2: handshake 2-RTT, supports many cipher suites (some insecure). TLS 1.3: handshake 1-RTT (0-RTT for resumption), removes insecure ciphers (RC4, DES, 3DES), only supports AEAD ciphers (AES-GCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305). Perfect forward secrecy REQUIRED in 1.3.

Front: Full backup vs Incremental vs Differential?
Back: Full: all data. Restore: need only last full. Incremental: changes since last backup (full OR incremental). Restore: need full + ALL incrementals. Differential: changes since last full. Restore: need full + last differential. Exam trap: incremental = fastest backup, slowest restore. Differential = moderate both.

Front: Everything should be automated: SOAR vs SIEM vs EDR?
Back: SIEM: log aggregation + correlation + alerting (Splunk, ELK). EDR: endpoint threat detection + response (CrowdStrike, Defender). SOAR: orchestrates automated response playbooks across SIEM/EDR/ticketing. Exam trap: SOAR is the automation layer on top of SIEM/EDR.

Front: Hot site vs Warm site vs Cold site?
Back: Hot site: fully redundant, real-time data sync, minutes RTO. Most expensive. Warm site: partially configured, near-RPO data sync, hours RTO. Moderate cost. Cold site: empty facility, no equipment, days-weeks RTO. Cheapest. Exam trap: RPO/RTO requirements determine site choice, not budget alone.
